newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Western Australia budgets for A$69.8 mln surplus.
newsitem.headline: Western Australia budgets for A$69.8 mln surplus.

text.p: Western Australia state will have a A$69.8 million budget operating surplus for the 1997/98 financial year ending June 30, according to the state budget released on Thursday.
State expenditures are forecast at A$6,979 million and revenues at A$7,049 million.
State Premier Richard Court said increasing demand for services and cutback in federal grants and in revenues left finances tight.
"The budget will remain in balance, however, because we have cut our cloth to meet our circumstances," he said.
Court said the only completely new revenue-raising measure was a gold royalty, although he said negotiations were underway with the timber industry to increase its royalties.
In addition:
- debits tax rates will double from July 1 in a move which will bring them into line with the other states.
- the payroll tax base will be broadened to take in all employee benefits including superannuation and non-cash benefits except for the major fringe benefits paid in remote areas.
- at the same time, payroll tax rates will be cut to offset the broadening in the tax base, and the exemption threshold will be increased a further A$50,000 to A$675,000.
- residential electricity tariffs will increase 3.75 percent, the first such increase in five years, but there will be no change in the tariffs for business customers.
- business customers of Alinta Gas will also be unaffected by an average increase of 3 per cent in gas accounts.
- water, sewerage and drainage rates will, in general, rise by four percent but restructuring of tariffs to remove business cross-subsidy of households will continue.

- public transport fares will rise over the next four years to increase the total amount currently collected from 28 percent of operating costs to the "typical" international level of 40 percent. Standard adult fares in 1997-98 will increase on average nine percent.
- the cost of drivers' licences, currently the lowest in Australia, will also rise from July 1 and traffic infringement fines will double.
Premier Court told Parliament Premier Court told Parliament the cuts in Commonwealth funding have been savage over recent years and now threatened the future of the Federation.
"The serious reduction in Commonwealth funding has been of major concern because Western Australians are now generating record tax revenues for Canberra," Court said.

"More than A$1.5 billion of taxes that are being raised by the Commonwealth Government from Western Australia now stays in Canberra and is not returned to the State in the form of funding for services.
"The 'grab for cash' attitude which prevails in Canberra is short-sighted and, if left unchecked, will ultimately cause the breakdown of the Federation.
"Western Australians should not and will not accept being financially penalised unduly by a central government at a time when they are generating record levels of wealth."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
